summary:
Summary of our project:
We developed Nomad, a physical six-wheel Mars exploration rover paired with a real-time Mars Rover Dashboard. The rover uses a 360° LiDAR scanner and environmental sensors to map unknown terrain and stream live telemetry over Wi-Fi to an interactive web interface. The challenge asks for a layered, integrated map and tool to help astronauts navigate Mars safely, avoid obstacles, and monitor environmental conditions. Our solution directly meets these objectives by:
• Layered Mapping & Telemetry: Our dashboard combines multiple data layers—spatial LiDAR occupancy grids, polar radar sweeps, proximity/clearance metrics, ambient temperature, and humidity—into one unified interface.
• Obstacle Avoidance & Route Safety: The LiDAR scans a 12-meter radius to detect large rock formations and hazards, building a real-time occupancy grid that distinguishes safe, traversable paths (light green) from obstacles (red).
Astronauts on Mars wear bulky spacesuits, carry heavy scientific gear, and face extreme hazards with delayed communication from Earth. Sending a scout rover ahead—or using its live map during a Marswalk—gives astronauts up-to-date situational awareness of terrain obstacles and climate conditions before they step into dangerous zones.
details:
Nomad explores uneven terrain, scans its surroundings, and renders a live map on a browser dashboard:

  • Mobility & Hardware: A 6-wheel rocker-bogie suspension system powered by six DC gear motors and a Cytron MDD10A motor driver traverses rough surfaces.
  • Dual-ESP32 Processing: To prevent lag, we split tasks across two ESP32 microcontrollers. One handles Bluetooth drive control, while the second reads 5-byte data packets from a 360° LiDAR sensor (at 460,800 baud) and temperature/humidity data from a DHT11 sensor.
  • Live Occupancy Grid: The ESP32 decodes distance and angle data, traces laser rays across a 400 × 400 grid (where each cell equals 4 cm), and pushes frames via WebSockets (port 81) to our web dashboard (port 80)
  • What benefits does it have?
  • Zero-Lag Reliability: Separating locomotion control from sensor processing onto two dedicated ESP32 boards ensures smooth driving and uninterrupted data streaming. [1]
  • Self-Recovering Mapping: If the LiDAR goes silent for 6 seconds, the firmware automatically restarts the scanning task, and repeated revolutions reinforce obstacle accuracy on the map. [1]
  • Modular & Cost-Effective: Built with standardized fasteners, modular subassemblies, and an accessible total prototyping cost of 13,758 EGP, making repairs and sensor upgrades fast and straightforward.

Our goal is to bridge the gap between robotic precursors and human planetary exploration. By turning raw sensor data into an intuitive, live survival map, Nomad reduces physical risk for astronauts, saves mission time, and serves as a scalable, low-cost platform for autonomous navigation research.

The Tools We Used:

  • Mechanical & CAD: SolidWorks for 3D modeling, Ansys for Finite Element Analysis (FEA) stress testing, CNC laser cutting and press-brake bending for the 1 mm AISI 1020 steel chassis, and FDM 3D printing (ABS) for vibration-damping bearing housings.
  • Electronics & Sensors: Dual ESP32 microcontrollers, LDROBOT LD19 / RPLIDAR C1 360° LiDAR, DHT11 climate sensor, Cytron MDD10A dual-channel motor driver, 6 DC gear motors, and an 11.1V 5200mAh 40C LiPo battery.
  • Software & Protocols: Embedded C++ (WebSockets and DHT libraries), UART serial communication, HTTP/WebSocket servers, and JavaScript for rendering the live browser dashboard

Instead of building a static software map using only pre-recorded orbital data, we built a complete end-to-end hardware and software ecosystem. Combining a classic planetary rocker-bogie suspension with a dual-ESP32 split-architecture and a real-time ray-tracing occupancy grid lets our rover actively generate the live "ground-truth" map astronauts need during a Marswalk

Dashboard Access and Additional Technical Resources:

"Dashboard Access Notice"

The Nomad dashboard is hosted locally by the rover's ESP32 and accessed through its Wi-Fi network at "http://192.168.4.1/". Therefore, the link cannot be accessed remotely through a regular internet connection, as it requires a direct connection to the rover's ESP32 network.

To allow judges to explore the dashboard interface, we have included screenshots showcasing its mapping visualization, LiDAR radar sweeps, obstacle detection, and environmental monitoring features.

Mapping and Code Documentation (PDF):

We have also provided a detailed technical PDF explaining how our mapping system works, including the processing of LiDAR measurements, occupancy grid generation, data visualization, and the software implementation behind the dashboard.

Technical Documentation: https://canva.link/jh0uys5ze6bhl1d

Testing and Validation

We tested Nomad's mobility and real-time monitoring capabilities together. During testing, the rover successfully moved while simultaneously collecting LiDAR distance and angle data, reading environmental sensor measurements, and updating its browser-based dashboard in real time.

We also evaluated the communication between the two ESP32 microcontrollers and the dashboard to verify that sensor processing and rover movement could operate concurrently.

Technical Documentation – Nomad Mars Rover:

We have prepared a comprehensive technical documentation PDF detailing the design, engineering, and development of Nomad.

The document covers the rover's mechanical structure, six-wheel rocker-bogie suspension, electronic components, dual-ESP32 architecture, LiDAR-based mapping system, sensor integration, firmware, and real-time web dashboard.

It provides further technical insight into how our physical rover and software work together to support safer planetary exploration.
